## Abstract

This EIP adds an [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request type and a predeploy contract with which the execution address in a validator's withdrawal credentials can commit 64 bytes of post-quantum (PQ) material for that validator. The consensus layer stores one `(validator_index, pq_data)` pair per validator in the beacon state. A later request from the same owner overwrites the earlier one. A second request type and predeploy contract let the execution address of an [EIP-7732](./eip-7732.md) builder commit 32 bytes of PQ material for that builder in the same way. For a validator the first 32 bytes, and for a builder all 32 bytes, are a lean eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (leanXMSS) public key. The contract accepts a registration only with a proof of possession of that key. This EIP gives a validator's other 32 bytes no meaning. A future fork that migrates Ethereum consensus to post-quantum signatures will define how they are used. The intended use of those 32 bytes is verifiable random function (VRF) data, which together with the public key is enough to verify messages signed with that key.

## Motivation

The BLS signatures used by Ethereum consensus are not secure against a sufficiently capable quantum computer. Once such an adversary is credible, a BLS signature no longer proves that a message came from the validator's owner. That includes any message that would announce a new post-quantum key. A migration is only safe if every validator has committed to its post-quantum material *before* BLS is considered broken, through a channel whose authenticity does not depend on BLS.

The execution address in a validator's withdrawal credentials provides such a channel today. It is the owner of the validator's funds, and [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md) and [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) already let it act on the validator through execution layer requests. This EIP adds one more such request. [EIP-7732](./eip-7732.md) builders also sign their bids with BLS keys and face the same problem. Their execution address, set from the withdrawal credentials of the builder deposit and already used to authorize [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) builder exits, provides the same kind of channel, so builders get an equivalent request. This EIP lets owners start registering post-quantum commitments now, long before the migration fork, while leaving the design of that fork completely open.

## Specification

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and [RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174).

The builder contract uses the same storage slots, minimum fee, fee update fraction and `EXCESS_INHIBITOR` as the validator contract.

The request type value MUST be unique across all active [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request types. `0x00` through `0x02` are used by Electra. `0x03` and `0x04` are the builder request types of [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md). `0x05` is claimed by the draft proposals [EIP-8148](./eip-8148.md) and [EIP-8205](./eip-8205.md). `0x06` and `0x07` are the first values not claimed by any proposal. The final values are coordinated in consensus-specs together with any other request types scheduled for the same fork.

### Execution layer

#### PQ registration request

The new PQ registration request is an [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request with type `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE` consisting of the following fields:

1. `source_address`: `Bytes20`
2. `validator_pubkey`: `Bytes48`
3. `pq_data`: `Bytes64`

The [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) encoding of a PQ registration request is as follows. The encoded request value is exactly what the contract returns.

```python
request_type = PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE
request_data = dequeue_pq_registration_requests()
```

Each record is 132 bytes (`source_address ++ validator_pubkey ++ pq_data`), and `request_data` is the concatenation of all dequeued records in queue order. This is exactly the concatenation of the fixed-size SSZ serializations of the consensus layer `PQRegistrationRequest` containers, in the same order.

#### PQ registration request contract

The contract has the same queue design as the [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) consolidation request contract, with one more storage slot per queued request to hold the larger record. Its fee state is maintained differently from [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md), [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) and [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md): the excess is updated by the add path, decaying with the number of blocks elapsed since the last request, rather than by the system call. The fee therefore depends only on the rate at which requests are added, and it is well defined before the system call starts running, so registrations can be queued as soon as the contract is deployed. As in [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md), the fee charged on each write already accounts for the requests added earlier in the same block, and a system call with non-empty calldata disables the queue. There is no Solidity-compatible ABI. The contract dispatches on the caller and on `calldatasize` alone, through three code paths:

1. Add PQ registration request: a call from any address other than `SYSTEM_ADDRESS` with exactly `2516` bytes of calldata.
2. Fee getter: a call from any address other than `SYSTEM_ADDRESS` with empty calldata returns the current fee.
3. System process: a call from `SYSTEM_ADDRESS` dequeues the PQ registration requests for the current block.

Calls that match none of these cases MUST revert.

The `2516` byte input of a PQ registration request is:

| Bytes | Field | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `0:48` | `validator_pubkey` | 48-byte BLS public key of the validator |
| `48:112` | `pq_data` | 64 bytes of post-quantum material |
| `112:2516` | `signature` | 2404-byte leanXMSS proof of possession |

A request whose proof of possession does not verify MUST revert.

The contract records `msg.sender` as `source_address`. It does not check that the BLS public key belongs to a validator or that `msg.sender` controls it. The consensus layer honors the request only when `source_address` equals the execution address in the validator's withdrawal credentials.

##### Add PQ registration request

If the call data input to the contract is exactly `2516` bytes, perform the following:

1. Ensure the queue is not disabled and enough ETH was sent to cover the current PQ registration request fee (`msg.value >= get_fee()`)
2. Ensure fewer than `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` requests have been added in the current block
3. Ensure the trailing signature is a valid leanXMSS proof of possession, as defined below
4. Store the fee state for the current block and increase the PQ registration request count by `1`
5. Insert a PQ registration request into the queue for the source address, validator public key and PQ data. The signature is not stored
6. Emit the accepted 132-byte record as an anonymous log (`LOG0`)

The proof of possession is a leanXMSS signature at leaf index `0` by the public key in `pq_data[0:32]`. The signed message is `keccak256(POP_DOMAIN ++ chain_id.to_bytes(32, 'big') ++ validator_pubkey ++ pq_data[0:32])`, where `POP_DOMAIN` is `keccak256("leanXMSS registration proof of possession v1")`. Verification is specified by [`LeanXmss.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/LeanXmss.sol).

Specifically, the functionality is defined in pseudocode as the function `add_pq_registration_request()`:

```python
POP_DOMAIN = keccak256("leanXMSS registration proof of possession v1")

def valid_proof_of_possession(Bytes48: bls_pubkey, Bytes32: xmss_pubkey, Bytes2404: signature) -> bool:
    """
    A leanXMSS signature at leaf 0 by xmss_pubkey over
    keccak256(POP_DOMAIN ++ chain_id.to_bytes(32, 'big') ++ bls_pubkey ++ xmss_pubkey).
    """
    message = keccak256(POP_DOMAIN ++ uint256(chain_id).to_bytes(32, 'big') ++ bls_pubkey ++ xmss_pubkey)
    return signature_index(signature) == 0 and leanxmss_verify(xmss_pubkey, message, signature)

def add_pq_registration_request(Bytes48: validator_pubkey, Bytes64: pq_data, Bytes2404: signature):
    """
    Add PQ registration request adds a new request to the PQ registration request queue,
    so long as a sufficient fee is provided and the proof of possession verifies.
    """

    excess, count = get_fee_state()

    # Verify sufficient fee was provided.
    fee = compute_fee(excess, count)
    require(msg.value >= fee, 'Insufficient value for fee')

    # Enforce the per-block limit on added requests.
    require(count < MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK, 'Block limit reached')

    # The signature binds the XMSS key to this BLS key on this chain. It is not stored.
    require(
        valid_proof_of_possession(validator_pubkey, pq_data[0:32], signature),
        'Invalid proof of possession'
    )

    # Store the fee state for the current block.
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, EXCESS_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_STORAGE_SLOT, excess)
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_COUNT_STORAGE_SLOT, count + 1)
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_LAST_BLOCK_STORAGE_SLOT, block.number)

    # Insert into queue.
    queue_tail_index = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT)
    queue_storage_slot = PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_STORAGE_OFFSET + queue_tail_index * 5
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot, msg.sender)
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 1, validator_pubkey[0:32])
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2, validator_pubkey[32:48] ++ pq_data[0:16])
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 3, pq_data[16:48])
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 4, pq_data[48:64])
    log0(msg.sender ++ validator_pubkey ++ pq_data)
    sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT, queue_tail_index + 1)
```

###### Fee calculation

The following pseudocode computes the cost of an individual PQ registration request from the stored fee state and the current block number.

```python
def get_fee_state() -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """
    Return the excess and the number of requests added in the current block,
    rolling the stored state forward if no request was added in this block yet.
    """
    excess = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, EXCESS_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_STORAGE_SLOT)
    require(excess != EXCESS_INHIBITOR, 'Inhibitor active')
    count = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_COUNT_STORAGE_SLOT)
    last_block = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_LAST_BLOCK_STORAGE_SLOT)

    if block.number != last_block:
        # Fold in the count of the last block with requests, and decay the
        # excess by the target for every block elapsed since then.
        decay = TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK * (block.number - last_block)
        excess = max(0, excess + count - decay)
        count = 0

    return excess, count

def get_fee() -> int:
    excess, count = get_fee_state()
    return compute_fee(excess, count)

def compute_fee(excess: int, count: int) -> int:
    # Account for the requests already added in the current block.
    if count > TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK:
        excess += count - TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK

    return fake_exponential(
        MIN_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_FEE,
        excess,
        PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_FEE_UPDATE_FRACTION
    )

def fake_exponential(factor: int, numerator: int, denominator: int) -> int:
    i = 1
    output = 0
    numerator_accum = factor * denominator
    while numerator_accum > 0:
        output += numerator_accum
        numerator_accum = (numerator_accum * numerator) // (denominator * i)
        i += 1
    return output // denominator
```

The update `max(0, excess + count - TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK * (block.number - last_block))` gives the same excess as applying the [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md) end-of-block update `max(0, excess + count - TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK)` once for the last block with requests and once, with a count of zero, for every block after it. It is computed when a request is added instead of by the system call, so it does not depend on the system call running. As in [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md), `compute_fee()` also adds the requests submitted earlier in the current block above `TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK`, so the fee rises within a block as soon as the target is exceeded. The fee, and any value sent above it, is left locked in the contract.

##### Fee getter

When the input to the contract is length zero and the caller is not `SYSTEM_ADDRESS`, interpret this as a get request for the current fee, i.e. the contract returns the result of `get_fee()`. The call MUST carry no value. A value-bearing fee getter call reverts.

##### System call

At the end of processing any execution block where this EIP is active (i.e. after processing all transactions), call `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` as `SYSTEM_ADDRESS` with no calldata. The invocation triggers the following:

* The contract's queue is updated based on the PQ registration requests dequeued, and the queue head/tail are reset if the queue has been cleared (`dequeue_pq_registration_requests()`)
* The excess inhibitor is set if the call carries calldata, and cleared if it is set and the call carries none (`update_excess_inhibitor()`)

Unlike [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md), [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) and [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md), the system call does not update the excess or reset the request count. The add path maintains both.

Each PQ registration request MUST appear in the [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) requests list in the exact order returned by `dequeue_pq_registration_requests()`.

A system call with non-empty calldata dequeues requests as usual but then stores `EXCESS_INHIBITOR` into the excess slot, disabling the queue: subsequent PQ registration requests and fee getter calls revert. The next system call with empty calldata resets the excess and the request count to zero and re-enables the queue. Under this EIP the system call is always made with empty calldata, so this path is unused. It is reserved for the future fork that consumes the registered material, which can use it to stop accepting registrations.

Additionally, the system call and the processing of that block MUST conform to the following:

* The call has a dedicated gas limit of `30_000_000`. Dequeuing `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` requests uses about 11,000,000 gas.
* Gas consumed by this call does not count against the block's overall gas usage.
* Both the gas limit assigned to the call and the gas consumed are excluded from any checks against the block's gas limit.
* The call does not follow [EIP-1559](./eip-1559.md) fee burn semantics: no value is transferred as part of this call.
* If there is no code at `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS`, the corresponding block **MUST** be marked invalid.
* If the call to the contract fails or returns an error, the block **MUST** be invalidated.

The functionality triggered by the system call is defined in pseudocode as the function `process_pq_registration_requests()`:

```python
###################
# Public function #
###################

def process_pq_registration_requests(calldata: bytes):
    reqs = dequeue_pq_registration_requests()
    update_excess_inhibitor(calldata)
    return ssz.serialize(reqs)

###########
# Helpers #
###########

class PQRegistrationRequest(object):
    source_address: Bytes20
    validator_pubkey: Bytes48
    pq_data: Bytes64

def dequeue_pq_registration_requests():
    queue_head_index = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_HEAD_STORAGE_SLOT)
    queue_tail_index = sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT)
    num_in_queue = queue_tail_index - queue_head_index
    num_dequeued = min(num_in_queue, MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK)

    reqs = []
    for i in range(num_dequeued):
        queue_storage_slot = PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_STORAGE_OFFSET + (queue_head_index + i) * 5
        source_address = address(sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot)[0:20])
        validator_pubkey = (
            sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 1)[0:32]
            + sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2)[0:16]
        )
        pq_data = (
            sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2)[16:32]
            + sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 3)[0:32]
            + sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 4)[0:16]
        )
        req = PQRegistrationRequest(
            source_address=Bytes20(source_address),
            validator_pubkey=Bytes48(validator_pubkey),
            pq_data=Bytes64(pq_data)
        )
        reqs.append(req)

    new_queue_head_index = queue_head_index + num_dequeued
    if new_queue_head_index == queue_tail_index:
        # Queue is empty, reset queue pointers
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_HEAD_STORAGE_SLOT, 0)
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT, 0)
    else:
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_HEAD_STORAGE_SLOT, new_queue_head_index)

    return reqs

def update_excess_inhibitor(calldata: bytes):
    # Any calldata disables the queue
    if len(calldata) > 0:
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, EXCESS_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_STORAGE_SLOT, EXCESS_INHIBITOR)
        return

    # A call with empty calldata re-enables a disabled queue with a fresh fee state
    if sload(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, EXCESS_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_STORAGE_SLOT) == EXCESS_INHIBITOR:
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, EXCESS_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_STORAGE_SLOT, 0)
        sstore(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_COUNT_STORAGE_SLOT, 0)
```

##### Bytecode

The contract source is [`PQValidatorRegistration.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/PQValidatorRegistration.sol), [`RegistrationQueue.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/RegistrationQueue.sol) and [`LeanXmss.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/LeanXmss.sol). `LeanXmss` is a library and its bytecode is inlined into the contract. The bytecode below is produced as described in the Reference Implementation. The fee computation uses the [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md) `fake_exponential` and the [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) in-block adjustment, with the excess update moved from the system call to the add path. The queue read and write paths follow the [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) consolidation request contract with one additional storage slot per queued request. The constants are the stored input size (`0x70`), the record size (`0x84`), the slots per queued request (`0x05`), the queue offset (`0x05`), `TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` (`0x80`), `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` (`0x0100`) and `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` (`0x0400`). The calldata is `0x9d4` bytes: the stored input followed by the `0x964`-byte signature.

##### Deployment

TBD. The contract will be deployed through the [EIP-7997](./eip-7997.md) `CREATE2` factory, and `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` will be fixed once the salt is chosen. The contract can be deployed well before the fork that activates this EIP. Its constructor does not set `EXCESS_INHIBITOR`, so requests can be queued as soon as it is deployed. They are dequeued, and processed by the consensus layer, once this EIP activates. If there is no code at `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` once this EIP is active, every block from activation onward MUST be invalid.

#### Builder PQ registration request

The new builder PQ registration request is an [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) request with type `PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE` consisting of the following fields:

1. `source_address`: `Bytes20`
2. `builder_pubkey`: `Bytes48`
3. `pq_data`: `Bytes32`

```python
request_type = PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE
request_data = dequeue_pq_builder_registration_requests()
```

Each record is 100 bytes (`source_address ++ builder_pubkey ++ pq_data`), and `request_data` is the concatenation of all dequeued records in queue order. This is exactly the concatenation of the fixed-size SSZ serializations of the consensus layer `PQBuilderRegistrationRequest` containers, in the same order.

#### Builder PQ registration request contract

The builder contract at `PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` behaves exactly like the validator contract above, with the following differences:

* Its constants are `MAX_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK`, `MAX_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` and `TARGET_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` instead of the validator ones.
* A request is exactly `2484` bytes of calldata, laid out below. `pq_data` is the XMSS public key, so the proof of possession is over `builder_pubkey ++ pq_data`. Each queued request occupies four storage slots instead of five.
* The consensus layer honors the request only when `source_address` equals the builder's `execution_address`.

| Bytes | Field | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `0:48` | `builder_pubkey` | 48-byte BLS public key of the builder |
| `48:80` | `pq_data` | 32-byte leanXMSS public key |
| `80:2484` | `signature` | 2404-byte leanXMSS proof of possession |

The contract checks the signature and then discards it. The signature is not stored.

The queue insertion and removal differ from the validator contract only in the storage layout of each request:

```python
def insert_pq_builder_registration_request(Bytes48: builder_pubkey, Bytes32: pq_data):
    queue_tail_index = sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT)
    queue_storage_slot = PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_STORAGE_OFFSET + queue_tail_index * 4
    sstore(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot, msg.sender)
    sstore(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 1, builder_pubkey[0:32])
    sstore(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2, builder_pubkey[32:48] ++ pq_data[0:16])
    sstore(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 3, pq_data[16:32])
    log0(msg.sender ++ builder_pubkey ++ pq_data)
    sstore(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_TAIL_STORAGE_SLOT, queue_tail_index + 1)

def read_pq_builder_registration_request(queue_index: int) -> PQBuilderRegistrationRequest:
    queue_storage_slot = PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_QUEUE_STORAGE_OFFSET + queue_index * 4
    source_address = address(sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot)[0:20])
    builder_pubkey = (
        sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 1)[0:32]
        + sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2)[0:16]
    )
    pq_data = (
        sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 2)[16:32]
        + sload(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS, queue_storage_slot + 3)[0:16]
    )
    return PQBuilderRegistrationRequest(
        source_address=Bytes20(source_address),
        builder_pubkey=Bytes48(builder_pubkey),
        pq_data=Bytes32(pq_data)
    )
```

At the end of processing any execution block where this EIP is active, after the system call to `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS`, call `PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` as `SYSTEM_ADDRESS` with no calldata, under the same rules as the validator contract's system call. Each builder PQ registration request MUST appear in the [EIP-7685](./eip-7685.md) requests list in the exact order returned by `dequeue_pq_builder_registration_requests()`.

##### Builder contract bytecode

The contract source is [`PQBuilderRegistration.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/PQBuilderRegistration.sol). It uses the same [`RegistrationQueue.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/RegistrationQueue.sol) and inlined [`LeanXmss.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/LeanXmss.sol) as the validator contract, and differs only in the constants and in the four-slot storage layout of each queued request. The constants are the stored input size (`0x50`), the record size (`0x64`), the slots per queued request (`0x04`), the queue offset (`0x05`), `TARGET_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` (`0x02`), `MAX_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` (`0x10`) and `MAX_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` (`0x10`). The calldata is `0x9b4` bytes: the stored input followed by the `0x964`-byte signature.

### Consensus layer

The minimum consensus layer changes are sketched below against the [EIP-7732](./eip-7732.md) (Gloas) specification. Under EIP-7732, execution requests are no longer part of the beacon block body. A payload's requests are carried in `ExecutionPayloadEnvelope.execution_requests`, committed to by the `execution_requests_root` of the builder's bid, and applied to the beacon state by `apply_parent_execution_payload` when the child block is processed. Adding a field to `ExecutionRequests` is therefore enough to carry the new request type through the envelope, the bid commitment and the child block.

#### New containers

```python
class PQRegistrationRequest(Container):
    source_address: ExecutionAddress
    validator_pubkey: BLSPubkey
    pq_data: ByteVector[64]

class PQRegistration(Container):
    validator_index: ValidatorIndex
    pq_data: ByteVector[64]

class PQBuilderRegistrationRequest(Container):
    source_address: ExecutionAddress
    builder_pubkey: BLSPubkey
    pq_data: Bytes32

class PQBuilderRegistration(Container):
    builder_pubkey: BLSPubkey
    pq_data: Bytes32
```

The SSZ serializations of `PQRegistrationRequest` and `PQBuilderRegistrationRequest` are the 132-byte and 100-byte records returned by the validator and builder contracts.

#### New types

```python
class PQRegistrationRequests(ProgressiveList[PQRegistrationRequest]):
    """
    The PQ registration requests pertaining to a single execution payload.
    """

class PQRegistrations(ProgressiveList[PQRegistration]):
    """
    The registered PQ material, at most one entry per validator.
    """

class PQBuilderRegistrationRequests(ProgressiveList[PQBuilderRegistrationRequest]):
    """
    The builder PQ registration requests pertaining to a single execution payload.
    """

class PQBuilderRegistrations(ProgressiveList[PQBuilderRegistration]):
    """
    The registered builder PQ material, at most one entry per builder public key.
    """
```

#### Modified containers

`ExecutionRequests` is extended with two new fields:

```python
class ExecutionRequests(ProgressiveContainer):
    ...
    pq_registrations: PQRegistrationRequests  # [New in EIP-8483]
    pq_builder_registrations: PQBuilderRegistrationRequests  # [New in EIP-8483]
```

`BeaconState` is extended with two new fields:

```python
class BeaconState(ProgressiveContainer):
    ...
    pq_registrations: PQRegistrations  # [New in EIP-8483]
    pq_builder_registrations: PQBuilderRegistrations  # [New in EIP-8483]
```

Both fields are initialized to empty lists at the fork.

#### Modified `get_execution_requests_list`

The pairs `(PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE, execution_requests.pq_registrations)` and `(PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_TYPE, execution_requests.pq_builder_registrations)` are appended, in this order, to the list of request types, and the execution requests parsing in the honest validator guide is extended accordingly.

#### Modified `apply_parent_execution_payload`

The number of PQ registration requests is bounded together with the other request types:

```python
assert len(requests.pq_registrations) <= MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_PAYLOAD
assert len(requests.pq_builder_registrations) <= MAX_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_PAYLOAD
```

and they are processed after the existing request types:

```python
    for_ops(requests.deposits, process_deposit_request)
    for_ops(requests.withdrawals, process_withdrawal_request)
    for_ops(requests.consolidations, process_consolidation_request)
    for_ops(requests.builder_deposits, process_builder_deposit_request)
    for_ops(requests.builder_exits, process_builder_exit_request)
    # [New in EIP-8483]
    for_ops(requests.pq_registrations, process_pq_registration_request)
    for_ops(requests.pq_builder_registrations, process_pq_builder_registration_request)
```

#### New `process_pq_registration_request`

```python
def process_pq_registration_request(
    state: BeaconState,
    pq_registration_request: PQRegistrationRequest,
) -> None:
    # Verify the validator exists
    validator_pubkeys = [v.pubkey for v in state.validators]
    request_pubkey = pq_registration_request.validator_pubkey
    if request_pubkey not in validator_pubkeys:
        return
    validator_index = ValidatorIndex(validator_pubkeys.index(request_pubkey))
    validator = state.validators[validator_index]

    # Verify the request comes from the validator's withdrawal address
    has_correct_credential = has_execution_withdrawal_credential(validator)
    is_correct_source_address = (
        validator.withdrawal_credentials[12:] == pq_registration_request.source_address
    )
    if not (has_correct_credential and is_correct_source_address):
        return

    # Overwrite an existing registration for this validator
    for registration in state.pq_registrations:
        if registration.validator_index == validator_index:
            registration.pq_data = pq_registration_request.pq_data
            return

    # Otherwise append a new registration
    state.pq_registrations.append(
        PQRegistration(
            validator_index=validator_index,
            pq_data=pq_registration_request.pq_data,
        )
    )
```

Invalid requests are ignored. No validator status is checked: pending, active, exited and slashed validators can all register PQ material, as long as the request comes from their withdrawal address.

*Note*: The linear scan over `state.pq_registrations` is for specification clarity. Clients SHOULD maintain a cache mapping validator indices to positions in `state.pq_registrations`, as they already do for validator public keys.

#### New `process_pq_builder_registration_request`

```python
def process_pq_builder_registration_request(
    state: BeaconState,
    pq_builder_registration_request: PQBuilderRegistrationRequest,
) -> None:
    # Verify the builder exists
    builder_pubkeys = [b.pubkey for b in state.builders]
    request_pubkey = pq_builder_registration_request.builder_pubkey
    if request_pubkey not in builder_pubkeys:
        return
    builder = state.builders[BuilderIndex(builder_pubkeys.index(request_pubkey))]

    # Verify the request comes from the builder's execution address
    if builder.execution_address != pq_builder_registration_request.source_address:
        return

    # Overwrite an existing registration for this builder public key
    for registration in state.pq_builder_registrations:
        if registration.builder_pubkey == request_pubkey:
            registration.pq_data = pq_builder_registration_request.pq_data
            return

    # Otherwise append a new registration
    state.pq_builder_registrations.append(
        PQBuilderRegistration(
            builder_pubkey=request_pubkey,
            pq_data=pq_builder_registration_request.pq_data,
        )
    )
```

As for validators, invalid requests are ignored and no builder status is checked. Unlike validator registrations, builder registrations are keyed by public key rather than by index, because builder indices are reused after a builder exits.

## Rationale

### The registered key is checked, and the rest stays open

The contract checks a leanXMSS proof of possession of the public key in the first 32 bytes. It does not specify how a later fork uses that key, or what a validator's other 32 bytes mean. The 64 bytes only need to be enough to later authenticate a message signed by the owner of the PQ key.
Two 32-byte words let the signing key and the VRF data be registered separately, so neither has to be folded into a single hash with the other. Choosing the scheme, the parameters and the activation flow is left to the fork that actually needs them, when research on post-quantum signature aggregation, VRFs and key formats will have progressed.

### Builder registrations

Builders sign bids and execution payload envelopes with BLS keys, so they need a post-quantum migration path as much as validators do. They do not take part in proposer selection or RANDAO, so they need no VRF data. A builder registration therefore carries 32 bytes, the leanXMSS public key, rather than 64.

Builders get their own request type and contract rather than a flag in the validator request. The two registries are distinct in the beacon state, with different authorization fields and different lifecycles, so a separate request keeps each consensus layer handler simple. A separate contract also gives builders their own fee market and limits: a rush of validator registrations ahead of the migration fork cannot price out the comparatively few builders, and the smaller builder limits match the much smaller builder set.

Builder registrations are stored by public key rather than by `BuilderIndex`. Builder indices are reused after a builder exits and is swept, so an index-keyed entry could be inherited by an unrelated new builder. Builder public keys are unique in the registry, and the builder set is small, so the extra 40 bytes per entry are negligible.

### Execution layer requests instead of a BLS-signed consensus layer message

A consensus layer operation signed with the validator's BLS key could carry the same data. This EIP uses an execution layer request instead, for the following reasons:

* **Built-in DoS protection.** Every request pays gas and the [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md) style dynamic fee, and the per-block maximum bounds the work in each block. A consensus layer operation would need its own gossip validation, inclusion limits and anti-spam rules.
* **Already implemented.** Consensus layer clients already process [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md), [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) and [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) requests, and execution layer clients already run their system calls. The contract reuses the [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) queue and the [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) fee and inhibitor logic, moving the excess update from the system call to the add path, and the consensus layer change is a single request handler modeled on `process_consolidation_request`.
* **The owner of the funds is the right authority.** The withdrawal address owns the stake. The BLS key is often held by a node operator rather than the owner, and it is exactly the key that becomes untrustworthy once quantum attacks are credible. Binding the PQ material to the withdrawal address puts it under the control of the party who stands to lose the funds.
* **Simplicity.** No new consensus signing domain, gossip topic or beacon block operation is needed. The proof of possession is checked by the execution layer contract, and the request travels in the existing `ExecutionRequests` container.
* **Flexibility.** Smart contract withdrawal addresses, such as those used by staking pools, can register material for many validators under arbitrary custom logic, including multisig or governance approval.

### Storing the data in the beacon state instead of an execution layer contract

The contract could simply keep the latest registration per validator in its own storage. However, the consumer of this data at the migration fork will be the consensus layer. Storing it in the beacon state means the consensus layer will have everything it needs at that fork without proofs against execution layer state or new cross-layer reads. The cost is at most 72 bytes per validator and 80 bytes per builder public key in the beacon state.

### Proof of possession, with the rest left unspecified

The contract requires a leanXMSS proof of possession of the public key in the first 32 bytes of `pq_data`, which is all of a builder's `pq_data`. The proof stops a registration from naming a key the registrant cannot sign with, and it binds that key to one BLS public key on one chain. It does not decide how a later fork uses the key. A validator's other 32 bytes stay opaque, so the migration fork can still choose any scheme that fits in those bytes. Validators who registered early can overwrite their registration if the scheme changes.

### Replacing instead of dropping existing registrations

A later valid request for the same validator overwrites the earlier registration instead of being ignored. This lets owners correct mistakes, such as a wrong commitment or a lost PQ secret key, and rotate their PQ material before the migration fork. The authority to overwrite is the same as the authority to register, so allowing replacement does not weaken the authorization model.

### A separate list instead of a new `Validator` field

The PQ material is stored as `(validator_index, pq_data)` pairs in a new `BeaconState` list rather than as a new field of the `Validator` container. Adding a field to `Validator` would touch one of the most heavily used and cached structures in consensus clients. It would affect the hashing, serialization and memory layout of every validator, and every client's validator-registry caches and database schemas, for data that nothing reads until a later fork. A separate list keeps this fork's changes to a new request handler and one new state field.

The `Validator` container will have to change anyway at the migration fork, when the registered material is used to register the validator's PQ public key and related data. That fork can then move the data from `pq_registrations` into the new validator structure in a single migration and drop the list, so the validator layout is changed once and not twice.

### Public key in the request, index in the state

The request identifies the validator by its public key, as [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md) and [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) requests do. This is the identifier owners and tooling already use, and it is unambiguous even if validator indices are reused in the future. The state stores the resolved `ValidatorIndex`, which is smaller than a public key.

### Validators with BLS withdrawal credentials

Validators with `0x00` (BLS) withdrawal credentials have no execution address and cannot register. They must first change to execution withdrawal credentials with a `BLSToExecutionChange`. This is the same requirement as in [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md).

### Fee mechanism

In [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md), [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) and [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) the excess and the per-block count are updated only by the system call at the end of each block. This contract is meant to be deployed, and to accept registrations, well before the fork that starts the system call. With the inherited design, nothing would reset the count or decay the excess before that fork. The fee would grow as `fake_exponential` of the total number of registrations ever made, exceeding 1 ETH after about 700 of them, far short of the hundreds of thousands of validators expected to register.

The contract therefore updates its fee state on the add path. The first request of each block folds the count of the previous block with requests into the excess and decays it by `TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` for every elapsed block. This yields the same excess as an end-of-block update would, without depending on the system call. The fee reflects only how fast requests are being added. In particular, it does not depend on the length of the queue: requests waiting for the consensus layer do not make new requests more expensive.

The contract keeps the two modifications that [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) makes to the [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md) design. Charging each write for the requests already added in the same block makes the fee respond immediately to a burst of submissions, instead of letting a single block absorb many requests at the previous block's price. The calldata-triggered inhibitor gives the migration fork a way to stop accepting registrations with no new predeploy and no change to the execution layer, by passing calldata to the existing system call. Unlike those contracts, the constructor does not set the inhibitor, so the queue is open from deployment.

`MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` additionally caps the number of requests added in a single block, bounding the storage any block can write to the queue independently of the fee.

### Parameter choices

Every validator is expected to register before the migration fork, and most registrations are expected to be queued before this EIP activates, so throughput matters more than for consolidations. With `TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK = 128`, about 920,000 registrations can be added per day (at 7,200 blocks per day) at close to the minimum fee. `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK = 256` bounds a single block. Sustained demand at that limit raises the fee by a factor of about `e**(128/17)`, about 1,900, per block, so the long-run add rate stays near the target.

`MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK = 1024` is the drain rate. It is set well above the add limit so that the backlog queued before activation drains quickly: a queue of one million registrations drains in about a thousand blocks, a few hours, even with new requests arriving at the target rate. The contract checks the proof of possession when the request is queued, so processing a request on the consensus layer requires no signature verification, only a public key lookup and a write. 1,024 requests add little block processing cost. They add at most 1,024 × 132 bytes, about 135 KB, to the execution requests of a payload, and dequeuing them uses about 11,700,000 gas of the system call's 30,000,000 gas limit.

The builder contract uses `TARGET_PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK = 2` and caps both the requests added and the requests dequeued per block at 16, like the [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) builder exit contract. That allows about 14,400 builder registrations per day at the minimum fee, far more than the size of the builder set.

## Backwards Compatibility

This EIP introduces backward incompatible changes to the block validation rule set and must be accompanied by a hard fork. On the execution layer it introduces two new contracts at previously empty addresses and two new request types. On the consensus layer it adds two fields to `ExecutionRequests` and two fields to `BeaconState`. Existing request types and validator flows are unchanged.

## Reference Implementation

The validator contract is [`PQValidatorRegistration.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/PQValidatorRegistration.sol) and the builder contract is [`PQBuilderRegistration.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/PQBuilderRegistration.sol). Both are Solidity 0.8.38 and share [`RegistrationQueue.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/RegistrationQueue.sol). The leanXMSS verifier, [`LeanXmss.sol`](../assets/eip-8483/LeanXmss.sol), is a library inlined into each contract. These sources are taken from [ethereum/pq-staking-contracts](https://github.com/ethereum/pq-staking-contracts/tree/main/contracts/src). The bytecode in this EIP is solc `0.8.38+commit.1835d247`, with the optimizer enabled for 1,000,000 runs, EVM version `osaka`, and the CBOR metadata trailer omitted.

## Security Considerations

### Authorization by source address

The contract records `msg.sender` as `source_address` and checks a leanXMSS proof of possession of the key being registered. The proof binds that key to the BLS public key and to this chain. It does not authorize the caller: the signature is not over `source_address`. As in [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md), the consensus layer check that `source_address` matches the validator's execution withdrawal credentials is the authorization. Without it, an arbitrary caller could overwrite any validator's PQ material by replaying an observed proof. For builders, the corresponding check is that `source_address` matches the builder's `execution_address`, as for [EIP-8282](./eip-8282.md) builder exits.

### Ignored requests

A request for an unknown public key, for a validator with BLS withdrawal credentials, or from an address other than the validator's withdrawal address is dropped by the consensus layer rather than re-queued. The fee is not refunded. In particular, a request processed by the consensus layer before the validator's deposit has been processed is ignored and must be resubmitted.

### Public PQ material

The `pq_data` and the proof of possession are public: they appear in calldata, and `pq_data` appears in the contract log and in the beacon state. `pq_data` MUST therefore be a public value, such as a public key and a commitment to related public data, and never secret key material. A third party can resubmit calldata it observed. The resubmission carries the third party's own address as `source_address` and is ignored by the consensus layer.

### Requests queued before activation

Requests can be queued as soon as the contract is deployed, but the consensus layer processes them only after this EIP activates, in queue order. All checks are made at processing time, not at submission time. A request is honored if, when it is processed, its public key belongs to a validator whose execution withdrawal credentials match `source_address`. A request whose validator has changed its withdrawal credentials in the meantime is ignored. If several queued requests target the same validator, the last valid one wins.

### Compromised withdrawal address

Whoever controls the withdrawal address can register or overwrite the PQ material of its validators. This gives no new power to an attacker who controls the withdrawal address, since that attacker can already withdraw the entire stake. Owners SHOULD check their registered material in the beacon state before the migration fork.

### Overwriting before the migration fork

Because registrations can be replaced, the material that counts is the material registered when the migration fork activates. The future fork MAY decide to ignore requests processed after a certain point, for example to stop a withdrawal address that is compromised late from replacing the material.

### Fee overpayment

Calls to the system contract require a fee payment defined by the current contract state. Overpaid fees are not returned to the caller. It is not generally possible to compute the exact required fee ahead of time. When adding a PQ registration request from a contract, the contract can read the current fee first and then pay exactly that amount, as described in [EIP-7251](./eip-7251.md). Note that the system contract uses the `CALLER` opcode, so the address that calls it must be the execution address in the validator's withdrawal credentials.

### State growth

There is at most one entry per validator in `state.pq_registrations`, of 72 bytes each, so the list is bounded by the validator registry. With one million validators, the list is at most about 72 MB. Repeated registrations for the same validator overwrite rather than grow the list.

The execution layer queue grows while requests are added before this EIP activates, or faster than `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK` once it is active. Its growth is bounded by `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_ADDED_PER_BLOCK` per block and, over longer periods, by the dynamic fee, which keeps the add rate near `TARGET_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK`. Each queued request occupies five storage slots in the contract, paid for by the gas of the add call.

### Processing cost

Each request needs a public key lookup and a lookup in `state.pq_registrations`. With the caches recommended above both are constant-time, and the number of requests per payload is bounded by `MAX_PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_PAYLOAD` (1,024).

### Validator index reuse

The state stores the validator index. If a future fork introduces validator index reuse, it MUST clear the `pq_registrations` entry of a reused index. Otherwise the new validator would inherit the previous validator's PQ material.

### Builder index reuse

Builder registrations are keyed by public key, so a builder that takes over a reused index does not inherit the previous builder's PQ material. An entry for an exited builder stays in `state.pq_builder_registrations`. If the same public key later registers as a new builder, possibly with a different execution address, the old entry applies to it until the new execution address overwrites it. The migration fork SHOULD account for this, for example by clearing the entries of builders that have exited.

The builder list holds at most one entry per builder public key that was ever registered and registered PQ material, 80 bytes each. Each entry requires a builder in the registry, so its growth is bounded by the cost of builder deposits.

### System call failure

Although the likelihood of a failed system call to `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` or `PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` is extremely low, the behavior in such cases is well-defined: the block is marked as invalid. This follows [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md#system-call-failure).

### Empty code failure

This EIP should not be activated if there is no code at `PQ_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS` or `PQ_BUILDER_REGISTRATION_REQUEST_PREDEPLOY_ADDRESS`. This is similar to the consideration in [EIP-7002](./eip-7002.md#empty-code-failure).
